children: She was only in Class 8 when she first saw something most adults overlook: The quiet crisis of India’s informal workers.
For the 13-year-old girl from Jaipur, that crisis had a name: ‘Invisibility’— the biggest barrier the country’s informal workforce continues to face.
It hit close to home — literally. Her family’s driver, a man she had known since birth, did not know his own date of birth. He had no birth certificate, had never even seen his Aadhaar card.

“That fact just scared me. A birthday is so special, it’s so important to our identity, and people like him don’t have access to such basic information. That just felt really sad,” says Ariana Agarwal.
“It was liberating, in a way. Seeing the problem in broad daylight — someone so close to me facing this — made me realise how big the problem really is, and that I had to do something,” she recounts.
Ariana Agarwal
Not an abstraction

Agarwal then started conducting surveys to understand issues such as social security, debt and financial literacy. For the next few days, she dived into research — reading up on what life looks like for informal and gig workers. That’s when it clicked: the informal economy is not some distant abstraction. It is all around her — in factory workers, street vendors, helpers at home, even her own driver.
“This is surrounding us every single day, and they don’t have access to the same devices and information as us,” she says. That realisation was the turning point for her.

After piecing together why her driver faced the issues he did, she began mapping government schemes available to informal workers like him — how they could access them and importantly, how to make them aware of their rights.

“I sent a Google form across my school, and received some great responses. I understood that a lot of people were also passionate about this issue. I connected with them and created a group, and then we started surveying informal workers in different regions,” Agarwal recalls.
In June 2024, she launched her initiative, the Informal Economy Index (IEI),  aiming to turn compassion into action and make India’s ‘invisible workers’ count. She was only 14 then.

The organisation relies on a large, cross-functional volunteer base spread across departments such as outreach, field surveys and social media. In total, Agarwal has managed between 60 and 100 volunteers at different times, though the number fluctuates because many juggle other commitments too. These volunteers come from a wide age range.

They built a comprehensive survey — questions spanning social security, debt, financial literacy and whether the respondents were migrant workers. Once the responses came in, the team could pinpoint the exact problems each worker faced. The survey generated what they called a ‘Vulnerability Score’; the higher the score, the more challenges a worker was juggling. Breaking that score down into its component parts helped them see where help was needed the most.

Seeking Inclusivity: The motive behind the IEI is to change the perception of informal workers from invisible beneficiaries to essential economic providers whose needs, contributions and aspirations should inform decision-making by the authorities

Then, one by one, they stepped in — connecting workers to government schemes, teaching them how to move towards debt freedom or running small classes on financial basics. After that, they collated the data district by district, State by State, and shared it with NGOs and government organisations, so decisions could be made with a clearer, grassroots-level view of the ground reality.

By combining grassroots data collection, digital technology and policy recommendations, the IEI has successfully helped create an evidence-based framework to improve financial inclusion, welfare access and economic resilience at scale for the informal workforce.
While existing interventions for informal workers largely stop at handouts — cash assistance, welfare schemes and livelihood support, the IEI platform flips that equation.
The vulnerability score for each worker, factoring in debt, migration status, financial inclusion and access to social protection, suggests personalised recommendations.
Bank account opening, government scheme eligibility, debt management guidance and connections to local support systems are the logical steps that follow.

“We have received a lot of support. For example, we did a session with Punjab National Bank for a few workers in Punjab on how informal workers can open bank accounts, and we got some really good results from there. That partnership with the bank went very well and was genuinely helpful. ACORN Foundation India gave us space where we could survey workers ourselves. ACORN has an office in Dharavi in Mumbai, so we were able to bring in a few informal workers there for a financial literacy session,” the 16-year-old said.
Working with NGOs

“All these NGOs actually implemented the model within their own systems and took the surveys themselves. They didn’t use our volunteers; they kept going independently. But we constantly checked in on how well it was going — asking for photos and results from the surveys, which come directly onto our dashboard. So it was a very smooth process,” she adds.

“With the government, it was more about access. For example, the District Collector of Jhunjhunu in Rajasthan gave me access to a new community — something I would not have looked at on my own, like sarpanches and panchayats. That just broadened my vision and also our scale.”

Seeking Inclusivity: The motive behind the IEI is to change the perception of informal workers from invisible beneficiaries to essential economic providers whose needs, contributions and aspirations should inform decision-making by the authorities

The Informal Economy Index has directly reached over 14,000 informal workers across 8-10 districts of eight States — Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Delhi, and Jammu & Kashmir.

This year, the organisation received a grant under “Festival of Hope” of International Baccalaureate, which helped it scale the operation further.  “One of the approaches of our work is to bring large scale mindset shifts across institutions and larger networks and we are particularly keen that our idea is also independently replicated. For, the growth of the idea is more important to us than just our own reach and scale. This is important to address the scale of the problem we are dealing with,” Agarwal points out.

The immediate priority, she says, is to position the Informal Economy Index not merely as a data platform but as an education and mindset-change tool that reshapes how institutions understand and engage with informal workers.

By embedding the IEI more deeply within networks of civil society organisations, businesses and government bodies, the aim is to shift the dominant perception of informal workers from invisible beneficiaries to essential economic actors whose needs, contributions and aspirations should inform decision-making.

Through stronger partnerships, the IEI can help organisations streamline processes, coordinate support more effectively and design interventions grounded in real-time evidence. At the systems level, it can enable governments to adopt more inclusive, responsive and data-driven policies for the informal economy.
Expanding reach

“Our immediate goal is to expand the IEI’s reach from more than 14,000 workers to 40,000 by the end of this year. Achieving this scale will depend on building partnerships that can embed the IEI within their existing programmes and networks. We will also use our current funding to expand welfare camps, literacy sessions and other targeted interventions informed by the needs and patterns identified through the IEI,” Agarwal emphasises.

“Ultimately, we want the IEI to evolve from a student-led initiative into a systems-change tool that enables existing institutions to understand, prioritise and support informal workers more effectively. For us, successful expansion would mean that the idea is adopted and carried forward by many organisations, rather than all implementation remaining dependent on our team.”

title: Informal Economy Index: Giving visibility to invisible gig workers
